title: How the Mediterranean Sea Dried Up

paragraphs.text: The Mediterranean is one of the most familiar seas on Earth. It covers about two and a half million square kilometers, and more than twenty countries have a coast on it. On average it is about one and a half kilometers deep, and in one trench off Greece it goes down more than five kilometers. Its only natural link to the open ocean is a gap about fourteen kilometers wide between Spain and Morocco, and only about three hundred meters deep at its shallowest point: the Strait of Gibraltar.

Average depth of the Mediterranean
Calypso Deep, off Greece: the Mediterranean's deepest point

shots.on_screen_text: The Strait of Gibraltar from the Space Shuttle

stat.label: Depth of the Strait of Gibraltar at its shallowest point

paragraphs.text: Six million years ago, almost none of that water was there. The link to the Atlantic closed, the sea evaporated, and the floor of the Mediterranean became a vast basin of salt, in places perhaps more than a kilometer below the level of the ocean next door. Then the Atlantic broke back in and refilled it, perhaps in less than two years. We know this because of salt under the sea floor, canyons buried under the Nile, and a drill ship that pulled up something nobody expected.

paragraphs.text: So how does a whole sea dry up, and how do you fill it again? And could it happen again? There is a twist, too: some scientists now think the sea fell much less far than the classic story says. To answer all of that, start where the scientists did: with salt, in a place where salt should not be.

shots.on_screen_text: A salt mine at Realmonte, Sicily
Rock salt forming in the Dead Sea

ask.text: Could the Mediterranean dry up again?

paragraphs.text: In the 1960s, ships surveying the Mediterranean with sound found something strange under the mud of the sea floor: a hard layer that bounced the sound straight back. Geologists called it the M reflector. Nobody knew what it was. In the summer of 1970 an American drill ship, the Glomar Challenger, set out to find out. It was part of the Deep Sea Drilling Project, which drilled holes in the ocean floor from a ship floating in water several kilometers deep. The ship held itself in place over the hole with thrusters, while a string of drill pipe kilometers long hung beneath it. The two chief scientists on that cruise, known as Leg 13, were William Ryan, an American, and Kenneth Hsü, a Swiss geologist born in China.

stat.label: A hard layer under the Mediterranean mud that echoed sound back

paragraphs.text: The drill came up with things nobody expected so deep under the sea. Under the normal sea-floor mud were layers of gypsum and rock salt. There were thin, wavy layers that looked like mats left by microbes in shallow, sun-warmed water. And some of the salt had a chicken-wire texture that geologists knew from the salt flats on the shore of the Persian Gulf, near Abu Dhabi, where it forms on dry land under a blazing sun.

shots.photo: File:Dead Sea Halite Terraces and Salt Crust Formations 02.jpg

stat.label: A salt texture known from desert salt flats, found in the cores
stat.source: Hsü, The Mediterranean Was a Desert (1983)

shots.on_screen_text: Salt flats on the Persian Gulf coast
Salt flats (sabkha) on the Abu Dhabi coast
A sabkha drying in the sun, Abu Dhabi

paragraphs.text: Why does that matter? Because salt like this does not form on the floor of a deep sea. It forms where seawater evaporates. Let a pool of seawater dry in the sun, and gypsum crystallizes first, once most of the water has gone. Rock salt only appears when roughly nine tenths of the water is gone. To lay down thick salt, a sea has to lose most of its water, again and again.

shots.on_screen_text: Evaporation ponds at the south end of the Dead Sea
Salt crystallizing in the Dead Sea
Salt pans by the Dead Sea

stat.label: Share of seawater that must evaporate before rock salt crystallizes

paragraphs.text: The Dead Sea, between Israel and Jordan, shows what that looks like today. Its shore is the lowest dry land on Earth, more than four hundred meters below sea level, and its water is so salty that salt crystals grow on the bottom and along the shore. It is also shrinking, by around a meter a year, because more water evaporates than flows in.

stat.label: The Dead Sea shore: the lowest dry land on Earth

shots.on_screen_text: Salt flats on the Dead Sea's southern shore

stat.label: How fast the Dead Sea's level has been falling

paragraphs.text: And there was a lot of it. Later surveys found that salt lies under almost the whole deep Mediterranean, in places more than a kilometer thick. Altogether, more than a million cubic kilometers of it. That is about five percent of all the salt dissolved in all the world's oceans today, taken out and laid down in one sea.

shots.photo: File:ISS035-E-007148 Nile - Sinai - Dead Sea - Wide Angle View.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The eastern Mediterranean from the space station

stat.label: Thickness of the salt layer in places
Salt from the crisis under the Mediterranean
Share of the ocean's dissolved salt now locked under the Mediterranean

shots.photo: File:Detail of rocks, Cabo de Gata, Andalusia, Spain.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Rocks of Cabo de Gata, Spain

paragraphs.text: In 1973 Hsü, Ryan and the Italian geologist Maria Bianca Cita published their explanation in Nature. The Mediterranean, they argued, had dried out, and not once, but over and over: a deep, hot, empty basin far below sea level, with salt lakes on its floor. Many scientists thought it was absurd. Some argued that the salt could have settled out at the bottom of a deep sea that never dried, filled with heavy brine. The argument went on for decades. Hsü later wrote a book about the expedition with a title that said it plainly: The Mediterranean Was a Desert.

stat.label: Hsü, Ryan and Cita: the Mediterranean dried out

shots.on_screen_text: Lake Assal, Djibouti: a salt lake below sea level today

stat.label: The rival idea: salt settling in a deep sea that never dried

shots.on_screen_text: Playa de Mónsul, Cabo de Gata, Spain

stat.label: Hsü's book The Mediterranean Was a Desert

shots.photo: File:Atlantis seen over the Mediterranean Sea, near the Algerian coast.jpeg

paragraphs.text: There was one more clue in the cores. Right on top of the salt, with no gap between them, lay ordinary deep-sea ooze, full of the tiny shells of creatures that live in the open ocean. Whatever had happened, it had ended suddenly. One moment the basin was making salt; the next, it was a deep sea again. That sudden switch would turn out to be the most dramatic part of the story.

stat.label: In the cores, open-ocean ooze lies right on top of the salt
stat.source: Hsü, The Mediterranean Was a Desert (1983)

stat.label: Single-celled creatures with shells, typical of the open ocean

shots.on_screen_text: The Rock of Gibraltar from orbit

paragraphs.text: So how do you cut off a sea? Today the Mediterranean loses more water to evaporation than all its rivers and rain put back. The hot, dry summers around it see to that. What keeps it full is the Atlantic. Through the Strait of Gibraltar, ocean water pours in at the surface, while heavier, saltier Mediterranean water slides out underneath. Close that door, and the sea starts to shrink. Scientists estimate that, cut off today, it would lose most of its water in roughly a thousand years.

shots.on_screen_text: Egypt's coast from the space station
The coast of Libya at Benghazi

stat.label: Salinity of the Mediterranean; the Atlantic outside is about 36
Time for most of the sea to evaporate if it were cut off today (estimate)

paragraphs.text: Six million years ago there was no Strait of Gibraltar. The Mediterranean was joined to the Atlantic through narrow seaways across what are now southern Spain and northern Morocco. And Africa was, as it still is, pushing slowly north into Europe. As the plates squeezed together, the land around those seaways rose. At the same time, ice was growing at the poles, and sea level around the world was falling.

shots.on_screen_text: The Granada basin, on the old Betic seaway
Northern Morocco, on the old Rifian seaway

stat.label: Growing ice sheets lowered sea level around the world

shots.photo: File:ISS035-E-007148 Nile - Sinai - Dead Sea - Wide Angle View.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The eastern Mediterranean from the space station

paragraphs.text: About five point nine six million years ago, the change began. A study published in Nature in 1999 dated it from layers of rock around the Mediterranean, and found that it started at the same moment everywhere. The gypsum in those rocks comes in repeated bands, and the bands follow slow wobbles in Earth's orbit. Count the bands, and you have a clock.

stat.label: Start of the salinity crisis, the same age across the basin

shots.on_screen_text: Gypsum bands of the Yesares member, Sorbas, Spain

stat.label: One wobble of Earth's axis (precession): one gypsum band

paragraphs.text: At first the sea did not vanish. For a few hundred thousand years, water still came in from the Atlantic, but not enough. The sea grew saltier, and gypsum settled out in the shallow basins along its edges. Then, around five point six million years ago, the link to the ocean was cut almost completely. Now the sea fell. Rivers kept flowing in, but the sun took more than they brought, and the level dropped and dropped. Salt piled up on the deep floor, layer after layer, as the brine shrank, refilled and shrank again.

stat.label: First stage: gypsum in shallow basins around the edges
The Mediterranean loses its link to the Atlantic, until 5.33

shots.on_screen_text: Salt forming in a shrinking sea: the Dead Sea

shots.photo: File:Dead Sea Halite Terraces and Salt Crust Formations 01.jpg

paragraphs.text: What would the dry basin have been like? Air that sinks warms up as it is squeezed, by about one degree Celsius for every hundred meters it goes down. A basin floor a kilometer below sea level would be about ten degrees hotter than the coast above it. Death Valley in California, less than a hundred meters below sea level, already holds the official record for the hottest air temperature ever measured.

stat.label: How much sinking dry air warms as it is compressed
Extra warmth on a floor 1 km below sea level (our calculation)

shots.on_screen_text: Badwater Basin, Death Valley, 86 m below sea level

stat.label: Highest air temperature on record, Death Valley, 1913

paragraphs.text: Near the very end, the water changed again. The last layers of the crisis hold the fossils of creatures from brackish lakes, the kind that lived in a great body of fresh and salty water that then stretched across Eastern Europe, ancestor of today's Black and Caspian Seas. Geologists call this phase the Lago Mare, the lake-sea. For a while, the Mediterranean was not a sea at all, but a chain of brackish lakes.

stat.label: The crisis's last stage: brackish lakes with eastern fauna

shots.photo: File:Detail of rocks, Cabo de Gata, Andalusia, Spain.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Rocks of Cabo de Gata, Spain

paragraphs.text: How far did it fall? On this map, the red is the sea floor that would lie bare if the Mediterranean dropped two hundred meters. At one and a half kilometers, the sea splits into separate salty lakes, and the Adriatic is gone entirely. Some geologists think parts of the basin fell even further. Others think the drop was smaller. We will come back to that, because the best evidence is buried under a river.

In the 1960s, Egypt began building the Aswan High Dam on the Nile. Engineers drilled into the riverbed to see what the dam would stand on. A Soviet geologist working there, I. S. Chumakov, found something odd. Under the Nile's sand and gravel lay a deep, narrow gorge cut into the rock, and the bottom of it held marine sediments, laid down by the sea, far from any coast. At the time it made little sense. It took the salt from the Glomar Challenger to explain it.

stat.label: Drilling for the Aswan High Dam finds a buried gorge under the Nile
Sea sediments found deep under the Nile at Aswan

shots.on_screen_text: The Nile valley north of Aswan

paragraphs.text: A river can only cut down as far as the water it flows into. If the Mediterranean had fallen far below the ocean, every river around it would have started cutting down too, chasing the falling shoreline. That is exactly what the Nile did. Its old canyon is still there, buried under the delta and the fields of Egypt. Near Cairo its floor lies about one and a half kilometers below the surface. Under the coast, it is about three kilometers down. That is deeper than the Grand Canyon, hidden under farmland and cities. Tens of millions of people now live on top of it, and most of them have no idea it is there.

shots.photo: File:The Nile River flows into the Mediterranean Sea (iss071e405499).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Nile flowing into the Mediterranean

chart.title: How deep the buried Nile canyon goes
chart.source: Communications Earth & Environment, 2022; US National Park Service

shots.on_screen_text: Tanta, in the middle of the delta

paragraphs.text: When the Atlantic came back, the sea flooded into these canyons. The Nile's gorge became a long, narrow arm of the sea, reaching far up into Egypt, all the way to around Aswan. That is why the drillers there found marine sediments. Over the next few million years, the river filled its old canyon with mud and sand, and built the flat delta on top.

shots.on_screen_text: The Nile valley in Middle Egypt

paragraphs.text: The Nile is not alone. Under the Rhône valley in France lies another buried canyon, hundreds of meters deep, found by drilling. Rivers elsewhere around the sea have them too. Each one is a record of how far down the sea went.

So how far? For decades the usual answer was: very far, maybe one and a half to two kilometers or more in parts of the basin. In 2022 a team studying the Nile canyon came to a smaller number. From the depth and slope of the buried canyon, they estimated that during that phase the sea fell by about six hundred meters. It is still a lot. Six hundred meters is enough to empty much of the shallow sea floor around the coasts. And it shows the debate is not settled.

stat.label: The classic estimate of the fall in parts of the basin
stat.source: Hsü, The Mediterranean Was a Desert (1983)

stat.label: Sea-level fall in one phase of the crisis, from the Nile canyon

shots.on_screen_text: Where the Nile valley opens into the delta

paragraphs.text: Then, five point three three million years ago, it ended. The Atlantic came back. Africa and Spain were still close together, but somewhere at the western end, a weak point gave way. We do not know exactly why. Perhaps the land sank, or perhaps a stream cutting back from the Atlantic side broke through. Seawater began to spill over a ridge of rock into the empty basin far below.

stat.label: The Atlantic returns: the Zanclean flood

shots.on_screen_text: Morocco's coast on the Atlantic side of the strait
The strait between Spain and Morocco

paragraphs.text: At first it may have been a trickle. But water flowing over rock cuts into it, and the deeper the cut, the more water flows through. In 2009, a team led by Daniel Garcia-Castellanos published a model in Nature. In it, the flow grew until it tore a channel about two hundred kilometers long through the sea floor between Spain and Morocco. It was less a single waterfall than a long, steep rapid, cutting its own bed ever deeper. Seismic surveys and boreholes had already found that channel, buried under later sediment.

shots.on_screen_text: Tarifa, at the strait's narrowest point

stat.label: Garcia-Castellanos and colleagues model the refill

shots.photo: File:Rock of Gibraltar in the clouds.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Rock of Gibraltar in the clouds
The narrowest part of the strait

paragraphs.text: And then it went very fast. In their model, about ninety percent of the water arrived in a period of a few months to two years. At its peak, the flow through the strait reached around a hundred million cubic meters every second. That is about five hundred times the flow of the Amazon, the biggest river on Earth. And the sea level inside the basin may have risen by more than ten meters a day.

stat.label: Share of the water refilled in a few months to two years, in the model
Peak flow through the strait in the model

chart.title: Peak flood flow against the Amazon
chart.source: Garcia-Castellanos et al., Nature 2009; Amazon average flow

paragraphs.text: Ten meters a day is about the height of a three-story building, every single day, across a sea the size of the Mediterranean. If the model is right, the floor of the Strait of Gibraltar is a scar of that flood: a channel cut in a few years, then drowned and left under the sea.

Picture the shore of a salty lake, far down in the dry basin. Week after week, the water climbs up the old slopes, ten meters a day, drowning salt flats, river valleys and canyons. The coastline you know today was being drawn in a matter of months.

shots.photo: File:Loma Pelada, Parque Natural Cabo de Gata - Nijar (26739960137).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Dry hills of Cabo de Gata, Spain

shots.photo: File:Panoramica del Cabo de Gata, Almeria (Almeria).jpg

paragraphs.text: Once the western basin was full, the water had to get over another barrier: the shallow sill between Sicily and Africa. Researchers have described what may be the marks of that second spill: a huge heap of flood debris at the foot of the Malta Escarpment, reported in 2018, and more than three hundred streamlined ridges across the Sicily sill, reported in 2024. If the flood happened this way, it poured from the western Mediterranean into the eastern half.

stat.label: Studies of possible flood marks off Malta and across the Sicily sill
stat.source: Micallef et al., Scientific Reports 2018; Communications Earth & Environment 2024

shots.on_screen_text: Southeastern Sicily, at the edge of the sill

paragraphs.text: Not everyone agrees. A 2020 review pointed out that other explanations are possible, and some researchers think the refill was slower or came in stages. But the core of the story is not in doubt. The Atlantic came back, and the age of salt was over. Geologists mark that moment as the start of a new chapter of Earth's history, the Pliocene, and its first stage is named the Zanclean, after Zancle, the ancient Greek name for Messina in Sicily.

stat.label: How fast the refill happened is still argued over
Start of the Pliocene and its first stage, the Zanclean

paragraphs.text: The salt is still there. Under the floor of the Mediterranean it lies buried beneath younger mud, and its age is named after Messina too: the Messinian. In Sicily, where the land has been pushed up since, the same salt is mined. At Realmonte, near Agrigento, miners dig rock salt that was laid down when the sea dried out.

stat.label: The age of the salt, named after Messina, Sicily

paragraphs.text: The same rocks gave Sicily another treasure. Sulfur formed in the gypsum of the crisis, and in the nineteenth century the island's sulfur mines supplied most of the world's sulfur, dug out by hand, often by children.

shots.on_screen_text: Old mining country near Caltanissetta, Sicily

stat.label: Sicily's sulfur mines lead world production

shots.on_screen_text: The hills of the Sicilian sulfur basin

paragraphs.text: In Spain, near Sorbas in Almería, you can walk through hills of gypsum from the crisis. Under the sea, the deep salt is so heavy and soft that it slowly flows, bending the layers above it. Off Israel, gas companies drilling for fields such as Leviathan, discovered in 2010, have had to drill through the salt to reach the gas below it.

stat.label: Buried salt creeps slowly, folding the rock above it
Gas field off Israel, below the Messinian salt

paragraphs.text: Could it happen again? The Mediterranean still needs the Atlantic to stay full. And Africa is still moving toward Europe, a few millimeters a year. Over millions of years, that could close the strait again. If it does, the sea will start to shrink, and in about a thousand years its deep basins will be lakes of brine once more. Nobody alive will see it. But the salt under the sea says it has happened before.

shots.photo: File:The International Space Station above the Mediterranean Sea (iss073e0767188).jpg

paragraphs.text: Put it together. Africa pushed north, the seaways closed, and the sun took the water faster than the rivers could bring it. More than a million cubic kilometers of salt were left on the floor. The rivers cut canyons down toward the falling shore. And then, five point three three million years ago, the Atlantic came back through Gibraltar, perhaps in less than two years. Every part of that story was pieced together from drill cores, buried canyons and salt.

stat.label: The refill in the Garcia-Castellanos model

shots.on_screen_text: A drill bit from the Glomar Challenger

paragraphs.text: So the next time you stand on a Mediterranean beach, think about what lies under the water. Below the blue, below the mud, is a layer of salt left by a sea that once nearly disappeared. Under the deltas are canyons cut by rivers that chased a falling sea. And at the western end is a channel torn open by one of the biggest floods we know of.

shots.on_screen_text: Playa de Mónsul, Cabo de Gata

shots.photo: File:Dead Sea Halite Terraces and Salt Crust Formations 02.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: The edge of the Nile delta

paragraphs.text: Here is my question for you. If you could stand on the floor of the dry Mediterranean six million years ago, where would you go first: down into the Nile canyon, out to the salt lakes of the deep basin, or to the edge at Gibraltar to watch the Atlantic come in?

shots.on_screen_text: Egypt and the Mediterranean from orbit

shots.photo: File:Rock of Gibraltar in the clouds.jpg

ask.text: Nile canyon, salt lakes, or Gibraltar?

youtube.title: How the Mediterranean Sea Dried Up
youtube.description: About six million years ago the Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic and almost completely dried out, leaving a deep basin floored with salt. This video follows the clues: the salt a drill ship pulled from under the sea floor in 1970, the canyon buried beneath the Nile, how far the sea fell, and the flood through Gibraltar that may have refilled it in less than two years. And could it happen again?
